<!-- conj-1: body_md -->
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, and $p$ be a prime where $E$ has good ordinary reduction. Then there exists a $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous elliptic curve $E'$ such that $\mu_{E',p}=0$.
<!-- end conj-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm1:Greenberg conj}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible as a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-representation. Then there exists a $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous elliptic curve $E'$ such that $\mu_{E',2}=0$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Assume $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible, them $\mu_{E,2}\leq 4$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm1: fine mu=0}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. Further suppose $E[2]$ is reducible. Let $R(E[p^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ be the dual of the fine Selmer group of $E[p^\infty]$ over $\mathbb{Q}_\infty$. Then $R(E[p^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ is $\Lambda$-torsion with $\mu$-invariant 0.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
Define the 2-primary Selmer groups to be \[\operatorname{Sel}(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\ker\Bigl(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])\to \prod_\eta H^1((\mathbb{Q}_\infty)_\eta, E[2^\infty])/\operatorname{im}(\kappa_\eta) \Bigr). \]
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop2: Equivalent definition}
An equivalent defintion of the 2-primary Selmer group over $\mathbb{Q}_\infty$ is \[\operatorname{Sel}(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\ker\Bigl(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])\to \prod_{l\in \Sigma} H_l(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])\Bigr). \]
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
This is in section 2 of \cite{Gr89}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
Define \[S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_{\infty})=\operatorname{Sel}^{\Sigma_0}(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\ker\Bigl( H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])\to \prod_{l\in \Sigma-\Sigma_0} H_l(\mathbb{Q}_\infty)\Bigr).\]
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
Define the non-primitive $2^n$-Selmer group to be \[S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\ker\Bigl(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])\to \prod_{\eta\in \Sigma-\Sigma_0} H^1((\mathbb{Q}_\infty)_\eta, E[2^n])/\operatorname{im}(\kappa_{n,\eta})\Bigr). \]
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop2: same mu}
$S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_{\infty})$ is $\Lambda$-cotorsion. The $\mu$-invariants of $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_{\infty})^\vee$ and $\operatorname{Sel}_2(E/\mathbb{Q}_{\infty})^\vee$ are equal.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is Corollary 2.3 in \cite{GV00}. \par
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
Define the 2-primary fine Selmer groups to be \[\operatorname{Sel}_0(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\ker(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])\to \prod_\eta H^1((\mathbb{Q}_\infty)_\eta, E[2^\infty]).\]
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem2: local expression at 2}
The local condition for $S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ at $p=2$ is $H^1(I_2, D_2[2^n])$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This is a generalization of Proposition 4.4 in \cite{Ma08}. For simplicity, set $F=\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,2}$, $F^{\operatorname{ur}}=\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,2}^{\operatorname{ur}}$. We need to show \[\ker\Bigl(g_2: H^1(F, E[2^n])\to H^1(F, E)\Bigr)\] is equivalent to \[\ker\Bigl(f_2:H^1(F, E[2^n])\to H^1(F^{\operatorname{ur}}, D_2[2^n])\Bigr).\] \\
As $D_2$ is divisible and $H^0(F, D_2)$ is finite, we can see that $H^1(F^{\operatorname{ur}}/F, D_2)=0$. Now by Proposition 4.3 in \cite{CG96}, we have \[\ker(g_2)=\ker\Bigl(H^1(F, E[p^n])\to H^1(F, D_2)\hookrightarrow H^1(F^{\operatorname{ur}}, D_2)\Bigr).\] On the other hand, since $H^0(F^{\operatorname{ur}}, D_2)=D_2$ is divisible, we conclude that \[\ker(f_2)=\ker(H^1(F, E[2^n]\to H^1(F^{\operatorname{ur}}, D_2[2])\hookrightarrow H^1(F^{\operatorname{ur}}, D_2).\] Therefore $\ker(f_2)=\ker(g_2)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem2: local expression at infty}
If $\Delta>0$, then the local condition for $S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ at an infinite prime $v$ is $H^1((\mathbb{Q}_\infty)_v, D_{\infty,v}[2^n])$. If $\Delta<0$, then the local condition at an infinite prime $v$ is 0.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The local condition is just the image of $E(\mathbb{R})/2^nE(\mathbb{R})$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2^n])$. Let $c$ be a complex conjugation induced by $v$, and $\left\langle P, Q \right\rangle$ be a basis of $E[4]$ over $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ such that $c$ acts as \[\begin{pmatrix}
-1 & t \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.\] If $\Delta>0$, then $2\mid t$, hence \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[4])=\left\langle P,2Q \right\rangle/\left\langle 2P \right\rangle, H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2])=\left\langle 2P, 2Q \right\rangle.\] On the other hand, $\operatorname{im}(\kappa_{1,\infty})=<2P>$ and $ \operatorname{im}(\kappa_{2,\infty})=\left\langle P \right\rangle$. Therefore, \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2^n])/\operatorname{im}(\kappa_{n,\infty})\cong \left\langle 2Q \right\rangle\cong H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty[2^n]).\] \\
If $\Delta<0$, then $2\nmid t$, hence \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[4])=H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2])=0.\] Therefore the local condition at $v$ is 0.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop2: description of E[4]}
If $\Delta>0$, then
\[S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)\cong \ker\Bigl(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])\to H^1(I_2, D_2[2^n])\times \prod_{v\mid \infty} H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_{\infty,v}[2^n])\Bigr).\]
If $\Delta<0$, then \[S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)\cong \ker\Bigl(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])\to H^1(I_2, D_2[2^n])\Bigr).\]
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This follows immediately from~\cref{lem2: local expression at 2} and~\cref{lem2: local expression at infty}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop2: inside outside}
The Selmer groups $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_{\infty})^\vee/(2^n)$ and $S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee$ have the same $\mu$-invariant.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem2: infinite compatible}
The natural inclusion $E[2^n]\hookrightarrow E[2^\infty]$ induces an isomorphism \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2^n])/\operatorname{im}(\kappa_{n,\infty})\cong H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty).\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By~\cref{lem2: local expression at infty}, we have \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2^n])/\operatorname{im}(\kappa_{n,\infty})\cong H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty[2^n]).\] But $D_\infty[2^n]\hookrightarrow D_\infty$ induces \[H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty[2^n])\cong H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty)[2^n]\cong H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty)\cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}.\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If $\Delta>0$, we consider the following commutative diagram 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 &0 \ar{d} & \\
 &H^0(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n]) \ar{d}& \\
S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty) \ar{r} \ar{d}& H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\Sigma}/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n]) \ar{r} \ar{d}& H^1(I_2, D_2[2^n])\times \prod_{\eta\mid \infty} H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty[2^n]) \ar{d}{\varphi} \\
S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)[2^n] \ar{r} & H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\Sigma}/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])[2^n] \ar{d} \ar{r} & H^1(I_2, D_2)[2^n] \times \prod_{\eta\mid \infty} H^1(\mathbb{R}, D_\infty)[2^n] \\
 & 0. & 
\end{tikzcd}\]
By~\cref{lem2: infinite compatible} and the fact $H^0(I_2, D_2)=D_2$(is a divisible set), $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. Now by the snake lemma, $S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ and $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)[2^n]$ differ by a finite set. Therefore, their duals have the same $\mu$-invariant. \par
If $\Delta<0$, we consider instead
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 &0 \ar{d} & \\
 &H^0(\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n]) \ar{d}& \\
S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty) \ar{r} \ar{d}& H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\Sigma}/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n]) \ar{r} \ar{d}& H^1(I_2, D_2[2^n]) \ar{d}{\varphi} \\
S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)[2^n] \ar{r} & H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\Sigma}/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])[2^n] \ar{d} \ar{r} & H^1(I_2, D_2)[2^n] \\
 & 0. & 
\end{tikzcd}\]
Now $\varphi$ is still an isomorphism, so as before, $S(E[2^n]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ and $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)[2^n]$ differ by a finite set.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop2: corank 1}
If $E[4]$ is reducible, then $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])$ has $\Lambda$-corank 1. Moreover, $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])/H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])_{\Lambda- \operatorname{div}}$ has $\mu$-invariant 1 if $\Delta>0$ and 0 if $\Delta<0$. In addition, the restriction map \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2])\to \prod_{\eta\mid \infty} H^1(\mathbb{R}, E[2]). \] is surjective. Also, if $\Theta$ is a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-module cyclic of order 2, then $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, \Theta)$ has $\Lambda/2\Lambda$-corank 1.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This is Proposition 5.8 and Lemma 5.9 of \cite{Gr99}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop2: mu of H1}
If $E[2]$ is reducible, then $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])^\vee$ has $\mu$-invariant $1+n$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Set $B=E(\mathbb{Q}_\infty)[2^\infty]$ and consider the following exact sequence \[0\to B/2^nB\to H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])\to H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])[2^n]\to 0.\]
Since $B$ is finite, $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^n])^\vee$ has the same $\mu$-invariant as $H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, \\ E[2^\infty])^\vee/(2^n)$. By~\cref{prop2: corank 1}, \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2^\infty])^\vee/(2^n)\sim \Lambda/(2^n)\oplus\Lambda/(2),\] which has $\mu$-invariant $n+1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop2: mu of Sel}
If $E[2]$ is reducible, then the $\mu$-factor of $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee$ is $\Lambda/(2^{\mu_E})$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Combining~\cref{prop2: corank 1} and \cref{prop2: mu of H1}, we see that the $\mu$-invariant of $S(E[2]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee$ is less than or equal to 1. Now combining~\cref{prop2: inside outside} with the structure theorem of finitely generated $\Lambda$-modules, we know that $S(E[2^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee$ has only 1 factor carrying the $\mu$-invariant.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
Let $\alpha$ be a finite $G_\mathbb{Q}$-submodule of $E[2^\infty]$, define \[\delta(\alpha)=\operatorname{ord}_2(\lvert F_2^+\alpha \rvert)-\operatorname{ord}_2(\lvert \alpha(\mathbb{Q}_v) \rvert)+\varepsilon_v(\alpha).\]
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm3: PR}
Let $E$ and $E'$ be two elliptic curves defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose we have the following exact sequence \[0\to \alpha\to E\to E'\to 0.\] Then we have \[\mu_E-\mu_{E'}=\delta(\alpha).\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
See Theorem 2.2 in \cite{Dr02}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop3: delta}
Let $\alpha$ be an order 2 $G_\mathbb{Q}$-submodule of $E[2^\infty]$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\alpha$ is odd and ramified, then $\delta(\alpha)=1$.
\item If $\alpha$ is not ramified and not odd, then $\delta(\alpha)=-1$.
\item Otherwise, $\delta(\alpha)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For the ramified part, notice that $\operatorname{ord}_2(\lvert F_2^+\alpha \rvert)=1$ if and only if $\alpha$ is odd, and it is 0 if and only if $\alpha$ is even.\par
For the remaining two terms in the definition of $\delta$. Let $\Delta$ be the discriminant of $E$, and $\rho: G_{\mathbb{Q}_\infty}\to \operatorname{Aut}(E[2^\infty]\simeq GL_2(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ be the representation on $E[2^\infty]$. Suppose $\Delta>0$, then for any infinite prime $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}_\infty$, the induced complex conjugation $c_v$ has image $\begin{pmatrix}
-1 & t \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ under $\rho$ with respect to a fixed basis, say $\{P,Q\}$, with $2\mid t$. Then $c_v$ acts on $E[2]$ trivially, hence $\alpha\subset E(\mathbb{Q}_v)$, and $\operatorname{ord}_2(\lvert \alpha(\mathbb{Q}_v) \rvert)=1$. Now $C_2=\left\langle P \right\rangle$, \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_v,\alpha)\simeq \alpha,\] and \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_v,E[2^\infty])\simeq \frac{P\otimes \mathbb{Q}_2/\mathbb{Z}_2\oplus Q/2}{P\otimes \mathbb{Q}_2/\mathbb{Z}_2},\] hence $\varepsilon_v(\alpha)=1$ if and only if $\alpha=\left\langle P/2 \right\rangle$ if and only if $\alpha$ is odd. \par
In the case $\Delta<0$, $c_v$ has image $\begin{pmatrix}
-1 & t \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ under $\rho$ with $2\nmid t$. Hence on the mod-2 level, the only $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant submodule is $\left\langle P/2 \right\rangle$, which implies that still $\operatorname{ord}_2(\lvert \alpha(\mathbb{Q}_v) \rvert)=1$. Since \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_v,\alpha)\simeq \alpha\] and \[H^1(\mathbb{Q}_v,E[2^\infty])=0,\] we have $\varepsilon_v(\alpha)=1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose $E[2]$ is reducible as a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-module and $C_2[2]$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant, then $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop4: K Im mu=0}
Assume all the assumptions in \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}. If $K$ is imaginary, then $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop4: K Re odd sub mu=0}
Assume all the assumptions in \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}. If $K$ is real and $\left\langle P \right\rangle$ is odd, then $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm4: Greenberg}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose $\Phi\subset E(\mathbb{Q})[2]$ is odd but not ramified, or not odd but ramified, then $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
This is Proposition 5.14 of \cite{Gr99}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Suppose the odd part of $E[2]$ is generated by $R$. Since $\tau$ acts on the odd part of $E[2^\infty]$ by $-1$, $\tau(R)=-R=R$ as $R$ has order 2. Therefore, according to the image of $\rho_2$, we have $R=P$. Since $\left\langle P \right\rangle$ is odd but not ramified, then according to \cref{thm4: Greenberg}, we have $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By the assumption, $\left\langle P \right\rangle\subset E(\mathbb{Q})[2]$ is odd but not ramified. Then by \cref{thm4: Greenberg}, $\mu_E=0$
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem4: 2 splits in K}
Assume all the assumptions listed above. Then 2 splits in $K$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Suppose not, then 2 is either ramified or inert in $K$. In either case, $\tau$ is in the decomposition field of $\mathbb{Q}_2$. Since $C_2[2]$ is $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$-invariant, according to the action of $\tau$ on $E[2]$, we must have $C_2[2]=\left\langle P \right\rangle$, contradicting our assumption.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm4: Greenberg Equivariant}
Assume $K\neq \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ a real quadratic field. Let $\Delta=\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$. Then \[\operatorname{Gal}(M_\infty/K_\infty)\sim \Lambda/2\Lambda[\Delta]\] as a $\Lambda[\Delta]$-module.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
This is Proposition 8 of \cite{Gr77}. The reason we need to exclude $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ is that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ is the first layer of the cyclotomic tower $\mathbb{Q}_\infty/\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem4: not Q(sqrt2)}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curved defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose $K:=\mathbb{Q}(E[2])$ is a real quadratic field, then $K\neq \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
In fact, we will prove $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{m})$ with $2\nmid m$. Let $y^2+a_1xy+a_3y=f(x)$ be a minimal Weierstrass form of our $E$. Using a change of variable if necessary, we have $E': y^2=g(x)$ with $g(x)\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ a cubic monic polynomial. According to chapter 3.1 of \cite{Si09}, there exists $u\in \mathbb{Q}^\times$ such that $\Delta_E=u^{12}\Delta_{E'}$ and $\mathbb{Q}(E[2])=\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])$. Hence we just need to show that $\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])\neq \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. \par
Since $\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])=\mathbb{Q}(E[2])$ is quadratic, then $\Delta_{E'}$ is not a square in $\mathbb{Q}^\times$, as otherwise $\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])=\mathbb{Q}$, which implies $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta_{E'}})$ is a quadratic field. Since $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta_{E'}})\subset \mathbb{Q}(E'[2])$, we have $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta_E})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta_{E'}})=\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])$. Since $E$ has good ordinary reduction at $p=2$, by the Ogg's formula about the discriminant and conductor (see 4.11.1 of \cite{Si94}), $2\nmid \Delta_E$. Therefore, $\mathbb{Q}(E'[2])=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta_E})$ is of the form $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{m})$ with $2\nmid m$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop4: K real not odd sub mu=0}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose $\Phi\subset E(\mathbb{Q})[2]$ is neither odd nor ramified and $\mathbb{Q}(E[2])$ is real and quadratic. Then $\mu_E=0$.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By \cref{prop2: inside outside} and \cref{prop2: mu of Sel}. It suffices to show $S(E[2]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee$ has $\mu$-invariant 0. By definition, we have \[S(E[2]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)=\operatorname{loc}_2^{-1}(H^1(I_2, C_2[2]))\bigcap (\cap_{w\mid \infty} \operatorname{loc}_w^{-1}(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, C_{\infty,w}[2]).\] We will analyze the two parts separately. \par
For the preimage of $\operatorname{loc}_2$, consider the following commutative diagram 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2]) \ar{d}{\operatorname{loc}_2} \ar{r}{f} & \operatorname{Hom}_\Delta(\operatorname{Gal}(M_\infty/K_\infty), E[2]) \ar{d}{\operatorname{loc}_\pi\times \operatorname{loc}_{\bar{\pi}}} \\
H^1(I_2,E[2]) \ar{r}{g} & H^1(I_2, E[2])\times H^1(\tau (I_2), E[2])
\end{tikzcd}\] with $f$ the restriction map, $\operatorname{loc}_\pi$ and $\operatorname{loc}_{\bar{\pi}}$ the corresponding localization maps. $g$ is the map $\sigma\to (\sigma, \tau^*(\sigma))$ with $\tau^*$ the conjugation map induced by $\tau$. According to theorem 25 in \cite{Iw73}, $I_2$ has $\mu$-invariant 1, then by \cref{thm4: Greenberg} and \cref{lem4: not Q(sqrt2)}, we may identify $I_2$ with $\Lambda/2\Lambda$ as a submodule of $\operatorname{Gal}(M_\infty/K_\infty)\sim \Lambda/2\Lambda[\Delta]$. According to inflation-restriction sequence, we have \[\ker(f)\simeq H^1(K_\infty/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2])\] and \[\operatorname{coker}(f)\hookrightarrow H^2(K_\infty/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2]).\] Hence both $\ker(f)$ and $\operatorname{coker}(f)$ are finite. Therefore, \[\operatorname{loc}_2^{-1}(H^1(I_2, C_2[2]))\sim \operatorname{loc}_\pi^{-1}(H^1(\Lambda/2\Lambda, \left\langle Q \right\rangle))\simeq \operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda/2\Lambda, E[2])=: N.\] \par
Next we consider the preimage of $\prod_{w\mid\infty} \operatorname{loc}_w$. Similar to the previous case, we consider the following commutative diagram \[\begin{tikzcd}
H^1(\mathbb{Q}_\Sigma/\mathbb{Q}_\infty, E[2]) \ar{d}{\prod \operatorname{loc}_w"} \ar{r}{f} & \operatorname{Hom}_\Delta(\operatorname{Gal}(M_\infty/K_\infty), E[2]) \ar{d} {\prod_w\operatorname{loc}_w\times \prod_w \operatorname{loc}_{\tau w}} \\
\prod_{w\mid \infty} H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w},E[2]) \ar{r}{h} & \prod_w H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, E[2])\times \prod_{\tau w} H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, E[2])
\end{tikzcd} \] with $f$ the restriction map and $h$ the map $\sigma_w\mapsto ((\sigma_w), \tau^*(\sigma_w))$. Let $M'_\infty$ be the maximal real subfield of $M_\infty$, then $\operatorname{Gal}(M_\infty/M'_\infty)\sim (\Lambda/2\Lambda)(1+\tau)$. Since still $\ker(f)$ and $\operatorname{coker}(f)$ are finite, we have \[\prod_w\operatorname{loc}_w(N)\sim \prod_{w\mid \infty} (H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, \left\langle P \right\rangle).\] Since $C_{\infty,w}[2]$ is either $\left\langle P+Q \right\rangle$ or $\left\langle Q \right\rangle$, we obtain that for any $w\mid \infty$ in $\mathbb{Q}_\infty$ \[\operatorname{loc}_w(N)\bigcap H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, C_{\infty,w}[2]).\] \par
However, according to \cref{prop2: corank 1}, $\prod_w \operatorname{loc}_w$ is surjective and $(\prod_w H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, E[2]))^\vee$ has $\mu$-invariant 1. Thus according to \cref{prop2: mu of H1}, we have \[N\cap (\cap_{w\mid \infty} \operatorname{loc}_w^{-1}(H^1(\mathbb{Q}_{\infty,w}, C_{\infty,w}[2])))\sim 0.\] Therefore, \[S(E[2]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)^\vee\sim 0.\]
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor4: mu<1}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Suppose $E[2]$ is reducible while $E[4]$ is irreducible. Then $\mu_E\leq 1$. $\mu_E=1$ if and only if $E[2]$ contains a $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant odd and ramified submodule $\Phi$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let $\Psi$ be the largest $\operatorname{G}_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant odd and ramified submodule of $E[p^\infty]$. Since $E[4]$ is irreducible, then $\lvert \Psi \rvert\leq 2$. Let $E'$ be the elliptic curve in the same isogeny class with $E$ and related to $E$ by the exact sequence \[0\to \Psi\to E\to E'\to 0.\] Then by \cref{prop3: delta}, we have $\mu_E-\mu_{E'}\leq 1$ and $\mu_E-\mu_{E'}=1$ if and only if $\Psi$ has order 2. \par
Let $C_{2,E}$ and $C_{2,E'}$ be the odd part of $E[2^\infty]$ and $E'[2^\infty]$ respectively. We claim that $C_{2,E'}=C_{2,E}/\Psi$. In fact, since $I_p$ acts on $C_{2,E}/\Psi$ by the cyclotomic character, then according to the classification of \cite{Se72}, $C_{2,E}/\Psi=C_{2,E'}$. Since $C_{2,E}[4]$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant, neither is $C_{2,E'}$. Therefore, according to \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}, $\mu_{E'}=0$. Combining this with the last paragraph, we have $\mu_E\leq 1$ and $\mu_E=1$ if and only if $\Psi$ has order 2.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm5: 16-isogeny}
Assume $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and has good reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible, then it admits at most a 16-isogeny.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
This is the main result in \cite{RZB15}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm5: Greenberg conj}
Assume $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible. Then there exists a $\mathbb{Q}$-isogenous elliptic curve $E'$ such that $\mu_{E'}=0$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Following the notations in \cref{cor4: mu<1}, let $C_{2,E}$ be the odd part of $E[2^\infty]$.
Let $\Phi$ be the largest ramified $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant submodule of $E[2^\infty]$. According to \cref{thm5: 16-isogeny}, such $\Phi$ exists with $\left\lvert \Phi \right\rvert\leq 16$. Say $\Phi$ has order $2^m$. Let $E'$ the elliptic curve in the same isogeny class with $E$, related to $E$ by the exact sequence \[0\to \Phi \to E\to E'\to 0.\] Since $C_{2,E'}[2]=C_{2,E}[2^{m+1}]/\Phi$, $C_{2,E'}[2]$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant, otherwise $C_{2,E}[2^{m+1}]$ is $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant, contradicting the assumption that $\Phi$ is the largest ramified invariant submodule. Therefore, by \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}, we conclude that $\mu_{E'}=0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm5: mu<=4}
Assume $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and has good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible, then $\mu_E\leq 4$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop5: mu_E<=n}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with good ordinary reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2^n]$ is reducible while $E[2^{n+1}]$ is irreducible for $n\geq 1$. Then $\mu_E\leq n$.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $\Phi$ be the largest possible ramified $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant cyclic submodule of $E[2^n]$. Then by assumption, $\Phi$ has order $\leq 2^n$. Let $E'$ be the elliptic curve in the same isogeny class as $E$ with \[ 0\to \Phi \to E\to E'\to 0.\] Then according to \cref{prop3: delta}, we have $0\leq \mu_E-\mu_{E'}\leq n$. Say $\Phi$ has order $2^m$, then by the same argument as in \cref{thm5: Greenberg conj}, $C_{2,E'}[2]=C_{2,E}[2^{m+1}]/\Phi$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant. Hence by \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}, $\mu_{E'}=0$. Therefore, we conclude that $\mu_E\leq n$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
According to \cref{thm5: 16-isogeny}, if $E[2^n]$ is reducible while $E[2^{n+1}]$ is irreducible, then $n\leq 4$. By \cref{prop5: mu_E<=n}, we have $\mu_E\leq 4$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm5: mu=m}
Assume $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and has good reduction at $p=2$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible, then $\mu_E=n$ if and only if the largest $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant ramified and odd subgroup $\Phi$ has order $2^n$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Suppose the largest $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant ramified and odd subgroup $\Phi$ has order $2^n$. Let $E'$ be the elliptic curve with the exact sequence \[0\to \Phi \to E\to E'\to 0.\] Then by \cref{prop3: delta}, we have $\mu_E-\mu_{E'}=n$. Since $C_{2,E'}[2]=C_{2,E}[2^{n+1}]/\Phi$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant, we have $\mu_{E'}=0$. Therefore $\mu_E=n$.
For the other direction, assume the largest $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant ramified and odd subgroup $\Phi$ has order $2^m$. Still consider the exact sequence \[0\to \Phi \to E\to E'\to 0.\] Then still by \cref{prop3: delta}, we have $\mu_E-\mu_{E'}=m$, so $\mu_{E'}=n-m$. However, on the other hand, according to our assumption, $C_{2,E'}[2]=C_{2,E}[2^{n+1}]/\Phi$ is not $G_\mathbb{Q}$-invariant. Thus by \cref{prop4: nonsplit mu=0}, we have $\mu_{E'}=0$, which implies that $n=m$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm5: Fine Selmer 0}
Assume $E$ is an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. Further assume $E[2]$ is reducible. Then $R(E[p^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}_\infty)$ is a finitely generated $\Lambda$-torsion module with $\mu$-invariant 0.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
In fact this result is exactly the version for $p=2$ of Corollary 3.6 in \cite{CS05}. Let $K(\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty]))$ denote the maximal unramified abelian $2$-extension of $\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty])$ in which every prime above 2 splits completely. Then still by Lemma 3.8 of \cite{CS05}, we have \[R(E[p^\infty]/\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty]))=\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Gal}(K(\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty]))/\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty])), E[p^\infty]),\] as $\mathbb{Q}(E[p^\infty])$ is complex due to the Weil pairing. Since $E[2]$ is reducible,  $\mathbb{Q}(E[2])$ is either $\mathbb{Q}$ or a quadratic extension. In either case, according to the main theorem of \cite{FW79}, the Iwasawa $\mu=0$ conjecture holds for $\mathbb{Q}(E[2])$. The rest follows from the proof of Theorem 3.4 of \cite{CS05}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
